interview_metadata.name: Jennifer Cuzzort
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Worcester, Massachusetts, and I have honestly never lived very far from here. I grew up in a pretty steady, middle-class household with my mom, dad, and my younger brother, and there was a lot of emphasis on being on time, doing what you said you would do, and not making a big scene about things. School was mostly fine for me. I was the kid who liked color-coded folders, neat handwriting, and checking things off a list, but I also worried a lot about getting things wrong. After high school I started community college, but I did not finish right away because money and work became the priority, so I took office jobs and found I was actually good at keeping schedules, files, spreadsheets, and front desks under control. I have never been married and I do not have children, so a lot of my adult life has been figuring out who I am outside of my family and trying to build a stable routine. I work as a general office clerk now, and I am planning to finish an associate degree in Business Administration because I want to move toward office management or project coordination. Outside of work, I read a lot, cook and bake, go for walks in Elm Park, do yoga, follow the Worcester Red Sox and Patriots, and keep a little indoor herb garden that probably gets more attention than some people give their pets.

follow_ups.question: When you think about your childhood in Worcester, what are the clearest everyday memories?
follow_ups.response: A lot of them are small things: walking to school with my brother, my mom reminding us to put our shoes by the door the night before, and going to farmers' markets on Saturdays when the weather was nice. We also had neighborhood block parties in the summer, where adults would bring folding chairs and kids would ride bikes up and down the street.

follow_ups.question: What made office work feel like a fit for you?
follow_ups.response: It rewarded the things I naturally do anyway. I like when a messy pile becomes an organized system, and I like being the person who knows where the form is, when the appointment is, and which spreadsheet has the right number.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was probably when I paused community college. I had started classes after high school thinking I would just keep going, but I was anxious about money and I did not feel like I had a clear direction. Around that same time I got a front desk job, first very basic phones and filing, and I realized I was more capable at work than I gave myself credit for. I could have pushed through school full time and taken on more debt, or I could work, slow down, and figure out what I actually wanted. I chose work first, and for a while I felt embarrassed about not having a degree. But over time it taught me that I am reliable and practical, and now I am returning to school part time with a better reason: I want business administration because it connects directly to the kind of supervisor role I want.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to before pausing school?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mom and one close friend from high school, Melissa. My mom was worried I would never go back, but she also understood that I was trying not to overextend myself financially.

follow_ups.question: What did a normal day look like during that transition?
follow_ups.response: I would work during the day, usually 8:30 to 5, then come home exhausted and look at course catalogs online. I remember making a spreadsheet comparing tuition, books, work hours, and bus schedules because that made the decision feel less emotional.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious, but not dramatic. I remember deciding that if I stayed in school while panicking about money, I would probably do badly at both school and work, so I gave myself permission to take the slower route.

follow_ups.question: Did you set any rule for yourself when you made that choice?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I told myself it was a pause, not quitting forever. I kept a folder with school information so it stayed like an open door.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about that decision now?
follow_ups.response: I feel more at peace with it now. I wish I had been less hard on myself, but I think the practical choice was right.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A clearer advising system at school would have helped. I did not really understand part-time pathways, financial aid details, or how to connect work experience to a degree plan.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have changed things?
follow_ups.response: Someone sitting with me for an hour and mapping credits, costs, and realistic timing would have made a difference. I needed specifics, not just encouragement.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone at work mentor you then?
follow_ups.response: Not formally, but an older administrative assistant named Karen showed me shortcuts in Excel and Outlook. She made office work feel like a skill set, not just a placeholder job.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am not married, I do not have children, and I am not living with a romantic partner. My parents are still in Worcester County, close enough that I see them pretty regularly, usually Sunday dinner a couple times a month. My mom is the person I call when I am spiraling about a practical decision, and my dad is quieter but very dependable. I have a younger brother, Brian, who is 24, and we are close in the way siblings are when they tease each other constantly but still show up. I have dated, but nothing has turned into a long-term partnership recently. Right now my family is important because they give me a sense of steadiness, but I also try to keep adult boundaries and not run every little decision through them.

follow_ups.question: What does a typical family visit look like?
follow_ups.response: Usually I go over on a Sunday afternoon, help my mom with salad or dishes, and my dad puts a game on in the background. We eat early, around 5, and then I head home before I get too tired for Monday.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk with your brother?
follow_ups.response: We text a few times a week, mostly jokes, sports stuff, or quick updates. We see each other maybe twice a month unless there is a family birthday or holiday.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: That is basically my immediate family: my mom, dad, and younger brother. I also have a couple of aunts and cousins nearby, but we are not in constant contact.

follow_ups.question: Do extended relatives gather for holidays?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually Thanksgiving or Christmas will include an aunt, an uncle, and a few cousins. It is friendly but not super intimate.

follow_ups.question: Who in the family are you closest to emotionally?
follow_ups.response: Probably my mom. She notices when I sound tense even if I say I am fine.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friend is Melissa, who I have known since high school. We usually get coffee or walk around Elm Park every other weekend, and she is the person who knows my overthinking patterns best. I also have two women from my yoga circle, Priya and Anna, who I would not call best friends yet, but they are important in my weekly life. At work, I am friendly with a coworker named Denise, and we sometimes eat lunch together in the break room. My social circle is not huge, but I prefer a few steady people over a lot of casual plans.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Melissa usually do together?
follow_ups.response: Coffee, walks, bookstore browsing, or sometimes we make dinner at one of our apartments. We are both low-key, so we do not need big plans.

follow_ups.question: How did the yoga friendships form?
follow_ups.response: Mostly from showing up at the same Saturday morning class and chatting afterward. Priya asked once about my sourdough starter, and somehow that turned into recipe swapping.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Worcester, in the 01605 area, in a rented two-bedroom apartment with a roommate. The neighborhood is mixed: some older triple-deckers, small apartment buildings, families who have been around a long time, and younger renters like me. I like that I can get to work, the library, grocery stores, Elm Park, and downtown without feeling totally isolated. It is not fancy, but it feels real and practical. There are seasonal farmers' markets and local events that make Worcester feel more connected than people sometimes give it credit for. I do hear traffic and sirens sometimes, and parking can be annoying, but I like having familiar places around me.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often near home?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, the library, Elm Park, and a coffee shop where I sometimes sit with a book. I also go to local theater performances when there is something affordable.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A little. I know the woman downstairs by name, and we text if a package gets delivered to the wrong door, but it is not a super close building.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe, especially during the day. At night I am more cautious, so I park close, keep my keys ready, and avoid walking alone too late.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you cautious?
follow_ups.response: Nothing directly to me, but there have been car break-ins nearby and occasional yelling outside late at night. It makes me aware of my surroundings.

follow_ups.question: Do you change your routine because of safety concerns?
follow_ups.response: A little. I do morning walks instead of late evening walks, and I check in with my roommate if I am coming home unusually late.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience and a sense of being rooted in Worcester. The downside is rent, parking, winter weather, and sometimes wishing the neighborhood were quieter.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from moving elsewhere?
follow_ups.response: My job, family, friends, and the fact that I know how to navigate Worcester. Starting over somewhere else sounds exciting but also expensive and stressful.

follow_ups.question: What would you change about the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Better sidewalks, more reliable snow clearing, and more affordable apartments that are actually maintained well.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live with one roommate, Rachel. She is 28 and works in a medical office, so we both have pretty regular weekday schedules. We each have our own bedroom and split the kitchen, living room, and bathroom. We are friendly but not attached at the hip, which works well for me because I need quiet time. We usually coordinate chores through a shared note on the fridge, and we split rent and utilities evenly.

follow_ups.question: How did you and Rachel become roommates?
follow_ups.response: A friend of a friend connected us when my previous lease was ending. We met for coffee first and talked through schedules, cleaning, and bills before agreeing.

follow_ups.question: What household chores are you usually responsible for?
follow_ups.response: I usually handle wiping counters, tracking shared supplies, and taking recycling out. Rachel is better about vacuuming and dealing with the bathroom.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent right now. It is just me and Rachel on the lease.

follow_ups.question: When does the lease renew?
follow_ups.response: It renews in the fall, so we usually start talking about it in late summer.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect the household to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not unless one of us gets a major job change.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: No one stays regularly. Rachel's sister has slept over once or twice, and Melissa has stayed after a late movie, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: Do guests affect household routines?
follow_ups.response: Not really. We usually give each other a heads-up by text.

follow_ups.question: Do family members ever stay over?
follow_ups.response: No, my family lives close enough that they just visit and go home.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one is away. Everyone who lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: Any pets away or shared pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets. I just have my herbs and succulents.

follow_ups.question: Any long-term travel planned by either of you?
follow_ups.response: No, just short weekend trips.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are pretty structured. I get up around 6:15, make coffee, check my calendar, and if the weather is decent I take a short walk before work. I work regular office hours, usually 8:30 to 5, then come home, make dinner, do laundry or errands, and read or do a puzzle before bed. Tuesdays and Thursdays I often do yoga or a short strength routine. Saturdays are more flexible: farmers' market, library volunteering sometimes, yoga circle, errands, or baking. Sundays are for meal prep, family dinner every couple weeks, and getting my planner ready for Monday.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:30 on weeknights. If I stay up later than that, I feel it the next day.

follow_ups.question: What do you meal prep most often?
follow_ups.response: Soup, roasted vegetables, rice bowls, salmon if it is on sale, and sometimes focaccia or sourdough if I have time.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a general office clerk for a small regional services office in Worcester. My schedule is Monday through Friday, usually 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with an hour lunch though I often take closer to thirty minutes if it is busy. I answer phones, greet visitors, enter data, process forms, keep files organized, help with scheduling, and do a lot of Excel tracking. I am also the person who notices when the copier is about to run out of toner or when a recurring report has a formula error. I do not currently have a second job, though I occasionally volunteer at the library.

follow_ups.question: What Excel work do you do most often?
follow_ups.response: Tracking appointment counts, budget lines, supply orders, and monthly reports. I use filters, pivot tables, conditional formatting, and lookup formulas pretty regularly.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you like least?
follow_ups.response: When people wait until the last minute and then everything becomes urgent. I can handle urgency, but preventable chaos wears me out.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my parents with online forms sometimes, like appointment portals, insurance paperwork, or anything that needs scanning and uploading. I also manage most of my own budgeting in a spreadsheet, and I update it every Sunday. I water my herbs and succulents every few days, depending on the plant, and I keep a running grocery list on my phone. When I am enrolled in classes, I block out two evenings a week for coursework because otherwise it gets swallowed by errands.

follow_ups.question: How often do your parents ask for paperwork help?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month. It is not overwhelming, but they know I am patient with forms.

follow_ups.question: What is in your budgeting spreadsheet?
follow_ups.response: Rent, utilities, groceries, transportation, subscriptions, savings, debt payments, and a small travel fund. I color-code anything that varies a lot.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is trying to be more consistent with morning walks and yoga instead of treating them like optional extras. I had a stretch last winter where I was getting tense and sleeping poorly, so I started putting walks on my calendar like appointments. I also restarted part-time school planning, so now some evenings are reserved for looking at course requirements and financial aid deadlines. At work, we changed a reporting process, so my mornings have become more spreadsheet-heavy.

follow_ups.question: What helped the morning walks stick?
follow_ups.response: Keeping my sneakers by the door and making the route short enough that I cannot talk myself out of it. Ten or fifteen minutes still counts.

follow_ups.question: Has the new reporting process changed your stress level?
follow_ups.response: A little, because I am responsible for catching errors. But I also like making the process cleaner, so it is stressful in a satisfying way.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me. My weekday routine is built around work, errands, exercise, and sometimes school planning rather than child care.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with any children in your family?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. I have younger cousins, but I am not responsible for their day-to-day care.

follow_ups.question: Does not having children affect your schedule flexibility?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it makes evenings more flexible, though I still feel like work and errands fill the time quickly.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My own experiences have been limited. I have gotten one speeding warning and one parking ticket, and I have called the non-emergency line once about a car that looked like it had been broken into. I have not had a serious personal encounter with police. I do notice policing more now than I used to, especially after the national conversations about race and police accountability. In Worcester, I think people have different experiences depending on neighborhood, race, and income, and I try not to assume my limited experience is universal.

follow_ups.question: How did the speeding warning go?
follow_ups.response: It was a few years ago on a local road when I was rushing to work. The officer was brief, gave me a warning, and I drove carefully afterward because I was embarrassed.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever attended a community meeting involving police?
follow_ups.response: No, not specifically. I have read local coverage, but I have not gone to a meeting.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing police at public events or traffic accidents. Nothing traumatic stands out personally, but I remember protests and conversations after 2020 making me think more critically.

follow_ups.question: Did those conversations happen in your family?
follow_ups.response: Some, yes. My family is pretty moderate and not everyone says things the same way, so I mostly listened and asked questions.

follow_ups.question: Do you follow local police news?
follow_ups.response: Only when it shows up in local news or community Facebook groups. I am not tracking it every day.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has either. I know of acquaintances who had DUIs or minor legal trouble, but no one close to me.

follow_ups.question: Has fear of legal trouble shaped your behavior?
follow_ups.response: I am rule-conscious generally, so yes in small ways. I pay tickets on time, keep documents organized, and do not like taking unnecessary risks.

follow_ups.question: Would you know where to turn if someone close to you was arrested?
follow_ups.response: I would probably call my parents first and then look for legal aid or an attorney. I would need guidance.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and most state elections, but I have missed smaller local elections before. I am trying to get better about municipal races because those decisions affect rent, schools, roads, and services here. I usually check my registration early, read a voter guide, and make notes in my phone before going. I do not enjoy political arguing, but I do think voting is a basic responsibility.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by mail or in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually in person because my polling place is manageable, but I have used mail voting when my work schedule was tighter.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk politics with?
follow_ups.response: Melissa sometimes, and occasionally my parents. I avoid getting into heated threads online.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as center-left or a moderate Democrat-leaning independent. I care about practical government: health care access, affordable housing, decent public schools, public transportation, and making sure people who work full time can actually live. I am not someone who wants politics to be my whole identity, and I get tired of constant outrage. At the same time, I do not think staying neutral is always fair when policies affect people differently. I tend to trust evidence, public health experts, librarians, teachers, and people working directly in services more than loud national personalities. I grew up with a pretty New England sense that you should contribute, not waste money, and not pretend problems disappear because they are uncomfortable. On social issues I am generally progressive, especially around LGBTQ rights, racial fairness, and reproductive health, but I am also cautious about slogans that do not explain how something will actually work.

follow_ups.question: What local issues matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Rent, road maintenance, library funding, public safety that feels fair, and keeping Worcester livable for people who are not making a huge salary.

follow_ups.question: What kind of candidate appeals to you?
follow_ups.response: Someone competent, specific, and not cruel. I like candidates who can explain budgets and tradeoffs without acting like every disagreement is evil.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more aware of housing and cost-of-living issues because rent is not abstract when you are paying it every month. I used to think of politics more as national elections and social issues, but now I pay more attention to city decisions and workplace policies. The pandemic also made me more appreciative of public health and basic administrative competence. I would not say my values changed completely, but they became more concrete and less theoretical.

follow_ups.question: What made housing feel more political to you?
follow_ups.response: Watching rent go up while wages do not move at the same pace. It makes you realize budgeting harder does not solve everything.

follow_ups.question: Did your workplace shape any political views?
follow_ups.response: Yes, seeing how much people depend on paperwork, deadlines, and benefits made me think about how complicated systems are for ordinary people.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me somewhat to a lot, mostly by making me more aware of things I did not have to think about growing up white in Worcester. I cannot say I experienced policing or racism the way Black people have described it, but listening to those stories made me realize how protected my assumptions were. It made me pay more attention to who gets treated as suspicious, who gets believed, and whose mistakes are seen as dangerous. I would not claim to be an activist, but I do think the movement pushed me to learn more and be less passive.

follow_ups.question: Where did you learn more about those issues?
follow_ups.response: Books, articles, local news, and conversations with friends. I also followed some public library reading lists because that felt more grounded than social media alone.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you talk with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a little. I try to be specific rather than accusatory, especially when someone says something too broad.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as both moral issues and systems issues. It is not just whether one person is nice or not racist in their heart; it is also about policies, enforcement patterns, school funding, housing, and who gets second chances. The hard part for me is wanting change but also wanting to understand the details of what reforms actually do. I support accountability, better training, mental health response options, and listening to communities that are most affected. I am still learning.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make the most sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Independent review when force is used, better data transparency, and having non-police responders for some mental health calls. Those sound practical to me.

follow_ups.question: What feels confusing or unresolved for you?
follow_ups.response: How cities balance immediate safety concerns with long-term trust. I know slogans are simpler than implementation.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I have been thinking about race as something that shows up in everyday systems, not only in obvious hateful moments. Worcester is diverse, but my own upbringing was mostly white and middle-class, so I know my experience was limited. I think a lot about education, housing, health care, and how wealth builds or does not build across generations. I also think white people can get defensive too quickly, including me sometimes internally, and that defensiveness can stop useful conversations. I am trying to listen more and not make myself the center of it.

follow_ups.question: Has living in Worcester shaped that thinking?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because different neighborhoods can feel like different worlds. You can see differences in housing, roads, school reputations, and access to services.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss race with coworkers?
follow_ups.response: Only carefully and occasionally. Work is not always the right place for deep political conversations, but sometimes current events come up.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly read, listened, donated small amounts when I could, and talked with friends and family. I did not join large protests, partly because crowds make me anxious and partly because I was cautious during COVID.

follow_ups.question: What kinds of donations did you make?
follow_ups.response: Small donations to a local mutual aid fund and once to a bail fund link a friend shared. Nothing huge, but it felt better than doing nothing.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed your media habits around race issues?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I try to read more than one source and include local voices rather than only national commentary.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My close friends are generally sympathetic to the issues, though not all equally active. Melissa talks about it in a thoughtful way and has gone to a couple local events. My parents are more cautious; they support fairness but sometimes worry that criticism of policing goes too far. My brother is more online and more blunt, so he gets frustrated with older relatives. I usually end up trying to slow the conversation down so it does not become people talking past each other.

follow_ups.question: Have any conversations changed someone's mind?
follow_ups.response: Maybe not dramatically, but my mom has become more open to talking about housing and school inequality. That feels like movement.

follow_ups.question: Do you avoid the topic with anyone?
follow_ups.response: Yes, with some extended relatives. I do not have the energy for every holiday to become a debate.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall my physical health is pretty good. I do not have a major chronic illness, and I try to stay active with walks, yoga, and some seasonal running or training plans. My bigger health issue is anxiety, mostly worry and tension rather than panic attacks every day. I sleep okay when my routine is steady, but stress can make me clench my jaw and wake up at night. I try to manage it with exercise, mindfulness, cooking, and keeping life organized.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any regular medication?
follow_ups.response: No daily prescription right now. I have talked with a doctor about anxiety, but I mostly use therapy-style coping tools and routine.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise in a normal week?
follow_ups.response: Usually three to five times, counting walks. Yoga is about once or twice a week when I am consistent.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Routine makes it easier. If I plan meals, set out walking clothes, and keep yoga on the calendar, I do pretty well. What makes it hard is winter darkness, work stress, and being tired after staring at spreadsheets all day. Money matters too, because healthy food and classes cost money, so I try to cook at home and use affordable community options.

follow_ups.question: What healthy meals do you rely on?
follow_ups.response: Salmon when I can afford it, lentil soup, roasted vegetables, yogurt, rice bowls, and salads with herbs from my windowsill.

follow_ups.question: What happens when the routine breaks?
follow_ups.response: I skip walks, order takeout, and stay up too late reading or scrolling. Then I have to reset on Sunday.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge like a broken bone or serious diagnosis. The main thing was finally admitting to my primary care doctor that anxiety was affecting my sleep and concentration. I had a few months where my shoulders were always tight, and I was waking up around 3 a.m. thinking about work tasks. My doctor suggested therapy resources, sleep hygiene, and keeping exercise consistent before jumping straight to medication. I have not solved it completely, but I am better at noticing the signs early.

follow_ups.question: Did you start therapy?
follow_ups.response: I did a few sessions through an employee assistance program. It helped, though I have not found a long-term therapist yet.

follow_ups.question: What are your early warning signs?
follow_ups.response: Jaw tension, rereading emails too many times, making unnecessary lists, and feeling like I cannot relax even when nothing is happening.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Anxiety can slow me down, but it has not stopped me from working. It mostly makes me overcheck things or feel drained after days with a lot of interruptions.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever taken sick time for it?
follow_ups.response: Once I took a mental health day and called it a sick day. I slept, cleaned a little, and reset my planner.

follow_ups.question: Does your manager know?
follow_ups.response: Not in detail. She knows I like clear deadlines and that too many last-minute changes stress me out.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: A little. My dad has high blood pressure, and my mom has had some back pain, so I worry about them as they get older. Nothing has required me to become a caregiver, but I help with appointments or online portals sometimes. My family is not very dramatic about health, which can be good, but it also means they sometimes understate things. I have learned to ask more specific questions instead of just asking if they are okay.

follow_ups.question: Who coordinates medical information in your family?
